title: Dynamic batch-shedding and KV-priority allocator to stabilize micro-batching under sustained QPS
creator: Aisha Banerjee
description:
Problem statement:

Under sustained high QPS spikes in production (customer workloads with short inference lifetime but bursty traffic), we observe the following combined failure modes:
- Micro-batching thresholds inflate to fill GPU throughput, causing longer queue latency and increased KV cache churn.
- KV cache eviction thrashing on the GPU leads to repeated KV loads, worsening memory pressure and occasionally triggering OOM or degraded kernel allocations.
- Static admission thresholds and simple backpressure heuristics do not adapt quickly enough to sudden QPS shifts, leading to unfair latency amplification across requests (longer-context requests push out short low-cost requests).

Goal:
Design and implement an adaptive "dynamic batch-shedding + KV-priority allocator" that:
1) Keeps p99/p995 latency within SLO during sustained QPS spikes;
2) Reduces GPU OOM events and kernel memory fragmentation;
3) Minimizes cost uplift by preferring cheaper degradation strategies (shedding, quantization fallback) over overprovisioning;
4) Provides an auditable canary rollout with observability for debugging decisions.

Proposed solution (high level):
- Dynamic batch-shedding controller: compute per-worker microbatch target using a short-window EWMA of queue latency, observed KV hit-rate, and GPU memory headroom. When memory headroom < X% or predicted queue delay > SLO, the controller selectively "sheds" (defers) low-priority requests from the fast path into a lower-priority lane or routes them to a quantized/approximate model variant. Shedding policy prioritizes: 1) non-interactive/low-urgency requests, 2) very long-context requests that inflate cache pressure, 3) requests from customers configured for best-effort.
- KV-priority allocator: maintain a small hot-set metadata structure per-GPU that assigns priority scores to KV entries based on recency, observed reuse rate, and request-criticality. Eviction then prefers cold & low-priority entries. When headroom permits, the allocator will prefetch and pin hot entries for upcoming predicted sequences.
- Asynchronous KV compaction and delayed freeing: instead of synchronous free on eviction (which can cause fragmentation), schedule compaction passes during idle micro-windows and use a fast deferred reclaim queue to batch frees.
- Fast-fallback quantization path: integrate a lightweight policy to reroute shed requests to a lower-precision kernel variant (mixed-int8 path) if available for the model, reducing memory pressure while preserving correctness for many workloads.

Implementation plan / milestones (epics):
1) Simulation harness (Week 1-2): extend the existing microbatching simulator to model dynamic shedding + KV-priority eviction. Validate across synthetic workloads and our replay traces from customer A (see artifacts).
2) Prototype controller + allocator (Week 2-4): implement controller in the serving runtime as feature-flagged logic; KV-priority metadata stored in a small device-resident ring buffer. Provide metrics endpoints.
3) Internal canary (Week 4): rollout to internal low-traffic cluster with aggressive telemetry (queue latency histogram by priority lane, KV hit/miss by priority, memory headroom events).
4) Customer canary (Week 5-6): staged rollout to 3 customers with different workload profiles. Gate by safety checks.
5) Full rollout + tuning (Week 7-8): integrate learnings, increase coverage, add operator-configurable knobs in Console.

Trade-offs considered and rationale:
- Aggressive global eviction: simple to implement but causes cold-cache misses and repeated reloads; measured to increase token cost by ~9% in replay tests. Rejected as primary strategy.
- Fixed headroom throttle: predictable but brittle; cannot differentiate between request priorities or context-length effects. Kept as a fallback safety guard.
- Per-request token reservations (reserve memory per incoming request): improves fairness but introduces allocation overhead and fragmentation. We'll implement a lightweight reservation token (small fixed-size ticket) instead of large reservations to reduce fragmentation risk.

Metrics & acceptance criteria (final):
- p99 latency: <= SLO + 10% under 3x baseline QPS sustained for 10 minutes.
- OOM events: reduced to zero for reproducible spike tests used by replay harness.
- KV hit-rate: no more than 5% degradation vs baseline for steady-state workloads; >10% improvement in hot-set retention for bursty traces.
- Cost: <= 6% increase in token compute cost for worst-case canary customers (ideally negative cost delta via fewer retries/less overprovisioning).

- Perf simulation outputs and traces: gs://redwood-perf/replays/2026-02/dynamic_shed_run_03.tar.gz
- Design doc: https://redwood.quip.com/UXYb/dynamic-batch-shedding-kv-priority (initial spec + algorithms)

Progress updates (timeline):
- 2026-03-02 (Aisha): ticket created after spike replayed from customer A. Reproduced OOMs on replay harness with default admission logic.
- 2026-03-04 (Luca): completed simulation harness extension; initial synthetic runs show dynamic-shedding reduces p99 by ~14% under 2.5x QPS synthetic trace. Added basic KV-priority scoring prototype.
- 2026-03-08 (Luca): wrote allocator prototype and small device-resident metadata ring. Early internal tests show KV hot-set retention improved ~12% for bursty traces. Observed minor regressive tail latency for priority lane when shedding ratio > 30% — added hedging policy.
- 2026-03-10 (SRE: Maya Chen): validated deferred free reduces fragmentation spikes during compaction windows. SRE requests safety knobs to force fallback to static throttle for customers with strict SLAs.
- 2026-03-12 (Aisha): finalized canary run checklist and created dashboard. Preparing PR for runtime integration (see PR link).

Open questions / next decisions required:
- Default shedding thresholds and tiering: what should be Redwood default vs. customer-configurable? (Proposal: conservative defaults, expose knobs in Console).
- Billing implications for shed requests: should shed->slow-path count towards customer token usage differently? Need legal/GO-TO-MARKET input.
- Priority source: combine customer-config labels + request-size heuristics + inferred urgency. Need to surface in API for customers who want control.

Acceptance tests to add to CI:
- Deterministic replay of three canonical bursty traces with and without dynamic-shed; assert no OOM, p99 within target.
- Stress test to assert deferred free does not cause long GC pauses on device.

Next immediate tasks (owners):
- Luca: land prototype PR and add metrics endpoints (ETA 2026-03-15).
- Aisha: coordinate canary customers and legal on billing semantics (ETA 2026-03-18).
- Maya (SRE): add operator kill switch and static throttle fallback (ETA 2026-03-16).
